The Yoshino Style Rules of Engagement is a martial art for armored warriors. When the heads of the senior Minato house were warriors, they passed the art to a single heir, together with the tsurugi.

Then the family gave up warrior status, and around the same time, this art also. From then on, the men of our branch inherited it: the priestess's husband, or a son who could not become the priestess himself.

Naturally, a warrior's art reached its full form in tsurugi combat. Fighting in the sky: that was the flower of the warrior's profession. But the flower was not the whole plant.

At the basic level, three branches. Swimming, unarmed combat, armored swordsmanship. Master those, then integrate them to learn tsurugi operation. After that came full certification.

Of the training, tsurugi operation took the smallest share. Nothing unusual there; other warrior schools were similar. Yoshino was not a famous school, but inside, its methods were quite ordinary.

Probably the difficulty of training with tsurugi explained this. Now, with mass-produced suits, group training was normal in the army. Before, a household usually had one suit only.

An experienced warrior demonstrating every movement beside a beginner—ideal, yes. Very rare. Direct practical instruction was not generally possible.

In another discipline, what a difficulty this would be. One boat available. One person fits inside. Kindly teach the novice to sail it. How much time and trouble would that require?

Yet the old records of warrior schools did not treat it as such a great obstacle.

Failures happened, of course. A man might master all the basics, put on the tsurugi, and fail even to fly properly. No certification for him, ever. Apparently, such people had existed.

<ruby>吉野御流合戦礼法<rt>よしのおんりゅうかっせんれいほう</rt></ruby>は武者の為の武術である。
　かつて皆斗本家の歴代当主が武者であった時代には、
劒冑と共にこの戦技も一子相伝されたと云う。

　が、皆斗家が士籍から離れると、ほぼ同時期にこの
武術も捨てられ、以後は湊斗家の男――巫姫の婿又は
巫姫たり得ない男児――が継承する慣わしとなった。

　武者の術であるから当然、その技法は劒冑を用いて
の騎航戦闘――武者の華たる空の戦いにおいて完成を
見る。
　といって、<ruby>それだけ<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>ということもない。

　吉野御流は基礎段階においては泳法、体術、そして
甲冑刀法の三系に大別される。
　これらすべてを習得すると、三系の統合に基く劒冑
操法を許され、皆伝免許となる。

　鍛錬の比重を問えばむしろ劒冑操法が最も少ない。
　これは武者<ruby>戦斗術<rt>れいほう</rt></ruby>の全般に見られる傾向で、珍しい
話では全くなかった。吉野御流は広く知られた流派で
こそないが、技法の内実はごく<ruby>標準的<rt>オーソドックス</rt></ruby>なものである。

　こうした傾向になる理由は、劒冑を用いた戦闘訓練
というものの難しさ――数打劒冑が量産される現在で
こそ武者の集団訓練は軍の常識となったが、かつては
一家に一領が普通であった――がそれであろう。

　武者が武者を手取り足取りに教えるという、理想的
な教育形態はごく珍しいものだった。
　それはつまり、経験者が未経験者に対して直接的な
実践教育を施せないということを意味する。

　他の技術であれば、これは致命的な問題ともなった
であろう。一隻しかない船の操法を素人に教える――
しかもその舟はごく小型で一人しか乗れないとなった
ら、果たしてどれほどの<ruby>手間隙<rt>てまひま</rt></ruby>が必要となることか？

　しかし武者武芸諸派の過去の記録を紐解くと、そこ
までの問題とはされていなかった事がわかる。

　無論、教授の失敗が無かったわけではなく。
　基礎を完全に習得しながら、劒冑を装甲すると満足
に飛ぶこともできず、遂に免許を得られなかった……
そういう者もいたらしい。

With a proper grounding in the basics, most learned to handle a tsurugi and fight in the air without much difficulty, even without an experienced pilot coaching them in practice. The foundation course was that complete. Unarmed training: learn to move the body. Swimming: learn to move through space, not just across a surface. Very few, though.

With a proper grounding in the basics, most learned to handle a tsurugi and fight in the air without much difficulty, even without an experienced pilot coaching them in practice. The foundation course was that complete.

Unarmed training: learn to move the body.
Swimming: learn to move through space, not just across a surface.
Armored swordsmanship: learn to fight inside armor.

Combine them, including combat practice underwater while wearing armor, and taking a tsurugi into the sky should cause little confusion. Faster, certainly. But much the same feeling.

...Or so the accepted wisdom went.

I had never worn a tsurugi. How much truth this wisdom contained, how far it missed—I was not qualified to give an opinion. Nor did I expect to become qualified in this lifetime.

Our Minato household was not a warrior lineage. Legally, we could neither possess nor operate a tsurugi. Practical experience was not going to present itself.

So in our Yoshino succession, the three basic arts came first. Then a formal transmission of secret teachings for the tsurugi we did not have. Training complete.

Chalaana aata hai? Do you know how to operate it? In theory, the knowledge is complete. Where is the thing? Not permitted. When did you last use it? That question is disrespectful to the entire arrangement.

Calling that a warrior's art might be rather presumptuous. At present, however, that was not my concern.

The family art included training that needed no tsurugi.◆ That part was what mattered to me now.

だがそういった話はごく稀だ。

　基礎を充分に身につけた者は、劒冑使用経験者から
実践指導を受けられずとも、大概さほどの困苦はなく
劒冑の操法を――空で戦う術を心得る。
　つまりは基礎課程の完成度がそれだけ高いのである。

　体術訓練において基本的な運体を学び、
　泳法において平面的ではなく空間的な運動を学び、
　甲冑刀法において装甲状態での戦い方を学ぶ。

　そしてその統合として、水中での着甲戦闘訓練まで
こなした者は、劒冑を得て空へ躍り出てもまず戸惑う
ことがない。
　速度差はあるにしても、感覚的にはほぼ同じなのだ。

　…………と。
　
　まあ、通念としてそういう事になっている。

　無論俺は劒冑を纏った経験など無いので、広く知ら
れているこの武術的常識がどの程度真実に近いのか、
また離れているのか、何も語れる立場にない。
　生涯そうだろう。

　そもそも湊斗家は武者の家系ではないから、劒冑の
所持運用を法的に許されない。
　実用経験など積むべくもなかった。

　吉野御流の継承は基礎三技術を習得後、形式として
劒冑使用を想定した秘伝の伝授を行い、完了する。
　これで武者の武術わざを称するなど、あるいは不遜とも
言えたろう。……が、そんな事はどうでも良かった。

　家伝の合戦礼法が、基礎修練として劒冑を用いない
武術も含んでいる――◆今の俺にとって意味があるのは、
そちらの方だ。

The most basic practice swing: a cut from the high guard, the proper starting position for a sword exchange.

In bamboo-sword kendo, or the unarmored swordsmanship behind it, high guard usually meant lifting the sword overhead. In warrior swordsmanship, the right shoulder was where it went.

Simple reason. Over the head, the helmet would object. Spend the stroke avoiding its horns, and what strength would remain to break another warrior's steel?

Not stepping had a reason also. A step shifted the body's weight and greatly increased the force of a cut. No argument there.

On the ground.
In the sky, that energy came from fast flight: the output of the Gattari, the precision of the horo, the advantage of greater altitude. Feet had no ground to apply themselves to.

On the ground, then, train what could still be used in the air. Arm strength. The spring of the upper body.
Hence this swing.

最も基本的な素振りだ。
　<ruby>太刀打<rt>タチウチ</rt></ruby>における正位、上段構からの斬りつけを想定
した鍛錬にあたる。

　竹刀を用いた競技剣道、あるいはその<ruby>基盤<rt>ベース</rt></ruby>となった
素肌剣術においては、上段といえば剣を頭上へ大きく
振りかぶった構を指すことが多い。
　が、武者剣法においてはこの右肩担ぎが上段である。

　理由は単純な事で、頭上へ振りかぶると兜が邪魔に
なるからだ。
　腕が兜の角に引っ掛からないよう注意しつつの上段
では、到底、武者の甲鉄を打ち破る剣など望めない。

　足の踏み込みを行わないのもまた、武者特有の条件
を踏まえての事であった。
　足の踏み込み……つまりは体重移動を行えば、剣撃
の威力は飛躍的に増す。これは、間違いない。

　だが、地上での話だ。
　空における体重移動の<ruby>力<rt>エネルギー</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>合当理<rt>バレル</rt></ruby>の出力と<ruby>母衣<rt>ウイング</rt></ruby>の
精度、そして<ruby>高度優勢<rt>ハイ・ポジション</rt></ruby>によって成し得る高速騎航から
生み出されるもの。足技の出番は無い。

　武者が地上において鍛えるべきは、空の打ち合いに
おいても活用可能な力――即ち腕力と上半身の<ruby>撥条<rt>バネ</rt></ruby>で
あった。
　従って、素振りはこの形になる。

Breathe in, raise the sword. Breathe out, cut down. The upper body worked with it: chest expanding forward on the rise, drawing back toward the spine on the cut.

Training for aerial sword combat, specifically. Useless on the ground, then? Not necessarily.

Masters of unarmored swordsmanship often said muscles were unnecessary. These warriors, always brute force, brute force. And indeed, the finesse of an art specialized for unarmored ground combat far exceeded a warrior's sword work.

Many stories told of the invincible terror of the skies meeting an elderly swordsman on the ground, without his tsurugi. One piece of firewood, and the sky's terror was thoroughly beaten.

But that was a master doing it.

吸気と共に振りかぶり、呼気と共に斬り下ろす。
　上体の収縮が、これに連動した。振りかぶる際は胸
を前方へ突き出すようにして膨らみ、振り下ろす時は
胸を背骨へ引き込むようにして縮む。

　これはあくまでも空の太刀打を想定した稽古である。
　しかし、地上戦において無意味かといえば――必ず
しもそうではなかった。

　しばしば、素肌剣術の達人は刀を扱うに筋力は不要
であると語り、力任せの武者刀法を嘲笑う。
　事実、地上の非装甲戦闘に特化された剣術の精妙さ
は武者の太刀業の比ではなく、

　空において剛勇無双を謳われた武者が地上で剣達者
の老人と劒冑を使わずに立合ったところ、<ruby>薪雑棒<rt>まきざっぽう</rt></ruby>一本
で叩きのめされた……などという逸話は数多い。
　が、それはあくまで、達人の域の話。

This time I stepped into the cut. Arm strength, chest and back, then the body's shifting weight on top.

Just before the wooden sword touched the earthen floor, I tightened my grip and stopped it. From the feel of that stroke, I judged its force. An opponent might brace firmly with a weapon of equal weight; I would probably still break through.

Let it miss by one hair. Turn aside enormous force with exquisite skill. Such things belonged to masters—or to the wonderful world inside an amateur's head. Saying them was the easy part. Against an ordinary opponent, they would hardly happen.

Warrior swordsmanship relied on force. But force was strength in its simplest form: easy to understand, easy to use. Unarmored technique was complicated. Perfect it, and perhaps nobody could beat you. First perfect it. Then keep mind and body in the condition required to use it.

As tools, the two differed in convenience. Better and worse were not so easily decided.

And warrior swordsmanship had techniques of its own, even if less intricate. Many worked on the ground too.

A flying dragon loses its tsurugi—its wings—and becomes a mole. People who disliked warriors loved that saying. I could not accept it as a proper account of the facts.

...Perhaps I was defending my own side. For a non-warrior like me, warrior swordsmanship had little purpose. An unarmored style would probably have served me better. Sensible conclusion. Very painful to agree with.

I could not go back and choose again. Even if I could, inheriting the family art had been my duty. Where was the choice?

Yoshino was the only road allowed to me. I did not want to conclude that the road went nowhere. For my peace of mind, such a conclusion was not recommended.

...But.
Put my feelings aside. Something still remained.

ものはある。

I knew how far a sword of brute force could go, if it took one wrong turn.

Wiping away sweat, I looked toward a corner of the dojo. A suit of armor and helmet stood on a small dais.

Cut cleanly in two.

A year it had stood like that. Too much to do. No time even to ask a smith to repair it.

...A year ago.
Yes. That time.

Even a surprise attack from here, she would stop easily. I admitted that to myself. Only a few years since I had begun teaching her Yoshino, and she had already gone past me.

No. From the beginning, really. The Head had refused her permission to learn; against custom, he said. Hikaru's response was to watch me and steal the techniques anyway.

Three days later she challenged me. And beat me.
My own talent was modest, granted. Even after allowing for that, what kind of ability was this?

The fact having arrived ahead of permission, the Head had been forced to approve. About two years of formal training later, she stood just short of the final certification. Unprecedented speed.

What had I taught her? Almost nothing. Three days watching me from cover, and she had surpassed me. Show her one thing; ten she understood.

So the feeling of being her master was rather thin. A student surpassing the teacher—whose credit was it, exactly? Not a kite giving birth to a hawk. A hawk had merely taken lodging with a kite, and the kite was trying to look responsible for it.

Proud, yes. As the brother of a genius, more than the master who had guided one. Her genius had not come from anything I had done.

But this last lesson, I had to teach her.
Not technique. The mind behind it.

Her figure blurred.

A lightning step.
A downward cut—

A battlefield sword with a convex, clamshell edge.
An iron suit of armor and helmet for the target.

　　　　　　　　　　　　Helmet Splitter

心中で、認めておく――今ここから不意に攻め掛か
ったとしても、苦も無く防がれるであろうと。
　光に吉野御流の手解きを始めてまだ数年……しかし、
実力は既に俺を凌いでいた。

　いや、それは最初からそうか。
　そもそも光が吉野御流の修行を希望した時、慣例に
反することだとして本家の許諾を得られなかったのだ
が――すると光は<ruby>勝手に<rt>・・・</rt></ruby>俺の技を盗み始め、

　<ruby>三日後<rt>・・・</rt></ruby>には俺に立合いを求めて打ち負かした。
　俺の凡才もあるが、それにしても異様な資質という
他はない。

　そうやって事実を先行させる形で強引に本家の承認
を得、正式に修練を開始して二年ばかり。
　前例の無い速度で、光は奥伝免許の手前まで至って
いた。

　実のところ、俺が教えた事など皆無に近い。
　物陰から三日間、俺の修行風景を眺めただけで俺の
技量を超えた光だ。その成長ぶりはまさに一を聞いて
十を知るというものだった。

　その為か、どうも光に対して師弟という意識が薄い。
　出藍の誉、と考えるにも複雑だ。<ruby>鳶<rt>とんび</rt></ruby>が鷹を生んだと
いうよりも、鷹がたまたま鳶のもとに居候したと表現
する方が適切に思える。

　誇らしくは感じるのだが、それはどちらかと言えば
弟子を導いた師としてではなく、天才の妹を持った兄
としての心情だった。
　天才の誕生において、己が何を為したとも思えない。

　しかし……最後に、この一つだけは、師として教え
ねばならないだろう。
　それは技術ではなく、心法に属する事柄であるが。

　光の後姿が霞んだ。

　瞬速の踏み込み。
　打ち下ろし――

　得物は<ruby>蛤刃<rt>はまぐりば</rt></ruby>の戦場太刀。
　据物は鉄の鎧兜。

　
　　　　　　　　　　　　兜割

A joke, from my side. No response from hers. Head down, deep in thought. Surely the poor quality of my joke was not the only cause. Her usual ease was gone.

It hurt. The school's rules required this, but still—I was deceiving my sister.

Helmet Splitter was the final trial for Yoshino certification. Give the student a thick-edged, heavy blade. Ask them to cut the armor and helmet completely in two.

Impossible from the start.
Armor was made not to be cut. That was its entire business.

Many masters had attempted the extraordinary feat of helmet splitting. Some had succeeded.

But not by cutting the thing in half. The most famous recent example, Kenkichi Sakakibara's demonstration before the Emperor, left a gash a little over nine centimeters across. That counted as success.

Properly, that was helmet splitting. Enough to kill the person inside. Even a sword saint could not cut deeper than that.

No need to halve it. No human ability to do so, either. And where Sakakibara and the others had used ordinary armor, Yoshino used a dead tsurugi.

Once, a favorite mount of the senior Minato house's head. Now dead, its supernatural powers gone. The steel's toughness remained. A tank could probably drive over it without leaving a dent.

A human body and a sword would not split that.
Impossible.

Impossible only.
The final examination ordered a person to do what could not be done.

甲鉄の頑強さだけは今も健在である。戦車で踏まれた
ところで凹みもつかないだろう。

　生身の人間の剣撃で斬り割れる筈がなかった。
　無理である。

　<ruby>無理<rt>・・</rt></ruby>、なのだ。
　この最後の試しは、できもしない事を命じるものな
のだ。

I looked away from Hikaru, toward the veranda. A swallowtail rested on a kumquat branch, softly moving its wings. Irresponsible little fellow. An unfair thought; what responsibility had a human assigned to a butterfly?

The test was not passed by splitting the armor.
It ended when the student gave up and admitted the limit of their own strength.

At the end of training, Yoshino did not demand superhuman power. It demanded the knowledge that one was not superhuman. Master the sword as far as you liked. Still a person only.

Giving up, not succeeding: that was the pass mark.

Nahin hoga, sir. I cannot do it. Excellent, you have passed. Continue announcing that you can, and the examiner must regretfully conclude that your understanding is incomplete. The sword may be sharp; the person holding it has still not reached the point.

Do not lose yourself in the power of the sword.

That warning was the test's real purpose.

...I did not think it was wrong.

Looking at those desperate eyes, I nearly let the truth slip. The school's rules forbade telling her. Of course they did.

A flexible mind might see the trick early. Hikaru's mind went straight at things. That sort of answer would not occur to her; I knew it.

Father had said the gifted stumbled hardest at this trial. For her, the highest wall of all. As a final examination, very suitable, if one wanted to be ironic.

Anyone carrying a sword needed this warning about power. Even so, from the examiner's side, I felt like a thoroughly nasty piece of work.
But the end should be near.

She had admitted her arrogance. She was beginning to know her limits. Stubborn girl, perhaps a little more time was needed. Eventually she would find the humility the founder required.

I believed in my sister.
That part was easy.

Did father mean nothing to her? Or did she not know what to feel about the word? Either way, painful.

Her father. My foster mother's husband. My foster father. He was no longer in the Minato household—in location or in law.

Soon after Hikaru's birth, he had left the family register, as good as driven out. He and the Head had often disagreed. Now he used his original surname and held a public post in Kamakura.

Once an heir to the priestess had arrived, perhaps the Head saw no further reason to keep the troublesome man nearby. To him, a Minato man was merely there to provide an heir.

So Hikaru had never met her father. They must have faced each other just after she was born, but surely she could remember nothing of it.

I still sometimes visited him in Kamakura. Hikaru had no such opportunity. The Head never approved of the daughter destined to be priestess leaving this district.

Father did not come here either. Busy, perhaps. Or perhaps he thought more about who would not welcome him than about who would.

But—

奇妙に感情のない声で、光が認める。

　父という単語に何も思うところがないのか……それ
とも何を思えば良いのかわからないのか。
　どちらであれ、痛ましい事だった。

　光の父――養母の夫――俺の養父――は、今現在、
湊斗家にはいない。
　それは単に座標的な意味においてもそうだし、また
法的な意味においてもそうだ。

　光が誕生してすぐ、しばしば本家と意見の食い違う
ことのあった養父は、追い出されるようにして湊斗家
から籍を抜いた。
　今は旧姓に戻し、鎌倉で公職に就いている。

　本家にしてみれば、湊斗巫姫の後継さえ出来たなら、
目障りな男をいつまでも身近に置いておく理由はもう
無かったのだろう。
　あのお人にとって、湊斗の男は種馬でしかない。

　だから、光は父に会ったことがなかった。
　出生直後に顔を合わせてはいる筈だが、まさか記憶
には残っていまい。

　俺は養父が家を出た後も時折鎌倉へ出向いて会う事
があったが、光にはそんな機会もなかった。
　巫姫たる娘がこの土地を離れる事に、本家は決して
良い顔をしないためだ。

　養父の方でも、ここへ近寄ろうとはしない。
　多忙のせいもあろう。……歓迎する人間の事より、
歓迎しない人間の事を考えてしまうせいもあろう。

　だが――

A quiet, level answer.
She wiped away the last sweat, set down the sword and took a wooden one instead.

Practice swings began. That pleasant sound of air being cut, regularly, again and again.

Already, the usual Hikaru.◆¦

A year ago, this had happened. For some reason I remembered the day clearly.

The next attempt should have been far more shocking. That day, though, was a blur in my memory.
Perhaps memory often did work like that...
